newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus turns down U.S. proposal on overflights.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus turns down U.S. proposal on overflights.

text.p: Cyprus rejected on Tuesday a U.S. proposal to ban Greek and Turkish military aircraft from flying over the divided Mediterranean island.

Cypriot Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told reporters his government could not enter an agreement with Turkey which implied that Ankara, which has occupied a third of the island since 1974, had rights over the island's airspace.

"We do not object to actions to reduce tension but they cannot have political implications as has the moratiorium (overflights ban) issue," Michaelides said after meeting the U.S. ambassador to Nicosia, Kenneth Brill.
The proposed ban has taken on added importance since Cyprus announced this month it would buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles, and Turkey responded with a threat of military action.
The rejection by Cyprus followed consultations President Glafcos Clerides held with the Greek government last week. Greece signed a military cooperation pact with Cyprus in 1993.
Cyprus has said, however, that it is willing to take unilateral steps, if necessary, to help a U.S. initiative to bring the divided Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities to talks this year.

Washington made its initial proposal to ban overflights late last year. U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh raised it again this month during a fleeting trip to the region to try to defuse the crisis over Cyprus's missile plan and Turkey's threatened response.

"We are disappointed that this opportunity to move forward has not been taken," Brill said. "We have had people taking far too many opportunities to move things backwards and it really is time to move the Cyprus issue in a positive direction."

Turkey invaded northern Cyprus in 1974 after a coup in the capital Nicosia engineered by the military government ruling in Athens at the time. Tension has risen on Cyprus since last summer when four Greek Cypriots and a Turkish Cypriot were killed in separate incidents along the U.N.-controlled buffer zone snaking through the island.

Brill said relations on the island could be improved if progress were achieved in U.N.-sponsored talks between the military commands of either side to disengage from some of their military positions, unload weapons and agree on a code of conduct along the ceasefire line.
